title: Menelaus in Higher Dimensions: The Signed Twisted-Cocycle Criterion
description: The Menelaus (transversal) dual of the parent's higher-dimensional Ceva cocycle. A hyperplane crossing the edges of an n-simplex and missing its vertices assigns each vertex i a nonzero value a_i and divides the edge i→j in the signed ratio m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j. These signed ratios obey a TWISTED cocycle law m(i,j)·m(j,k) = -m(i,k) and multiply to -1 around every triangular 2-face (classical Menelaus collinearity), versus the +1 of concurrent cevians. Conversely any nonzero twisted cocycle is reconstructed from vertex values a_i = 1/m(b,i), giving a transversal-hyperplane criterion m(i,j)·m(j,k)·m(k,i) = -1 on every 2-face. The duality m(i,j) = -r(j,i) shows Ceva (+1) and Menelaus (-1) are one identity up to sign.

overview.historicalContext: Menelaus's theorem (Menelaus of Alexandria, c. 100 AD) is the projective companion of Ceva's: for a triangle ABC and a transversal line meeting the (extended) sides at X, Y, Z, the three points are collinear iff the product of signed side ratios equals -1 — exactly the opposite sign to Ceva's +1 for concurrent cevians. The parent file CevasTheoremOQ02OQ04.lean answered open question 4 of cevas-theorem-oq-02 ('when do hypersurfaces bisect a simplex concurrently?') by identifying the planar Ceva product as a 1-cocycle on the simplex's edge ratios. This entry develops the dual transversal story: what replaces Ceva's cocycle when a hyperplane, rather than a point, crosses the simplex.
overview.problemStatement:
**Setup.** A hyperplane H = {x : ℓ(x) = c} missing every vertex of an n-simplex assigns each vertex i the nonzero value a_i = ℓ(V_i) - c. The point where H meets the edge from V_i to V_j divides it in the signed ratio m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j (the point (1-t)V_i + tV_j with ℓ = c sits at t = a_i/(a_i - a_j), giving t/(1-t) = -a_i/a_j).

**Theorem (forward).** The signed ratios satisfy the twisted cocycle law m(i,j)·m(j,k) = -m(i,k), and the product around every triangular 2-face is -1 (classical Menelaus collinearity); more generally the product around a closed walk of length L is (-1)^L.

**Theorem (converse / reconstruction).** Any nonzero signed assignment obeying the twisted cocycle law comes from vertex values: there exist nonzero a with m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j, given explicitly by a_i = 1/m(b,i).

**Transversal criterion.** For nonzero m the following are equivalent: (1) a transversal hyperplane realizing m exists; (2) m satisfies the twisted cocycle law; (3) the Menelaus product m(i,j)·m(j,k)·m(k,i) = -1 holds on every triangular 2-face.
overview.text: Higher-dimensional Menelaus's theorem via the signed twisted-cocycle criterion for simplex transversals. A hyperplane's signed edge ratios m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j satisfy m(i,j)·m(j,k) = -m(i,k) and multiply to -1 around every 2-face; conversely any nonzero twisted cocycle is reconstructed from vertex values a_i = 1/m(b,i). The duality m(i,j) = -r(j,i) makes Menelaus (-1) and the parent's Ceva (+1) one identity up to sign.
overview.proofStrategy:
The argument mirrors the parent's Ceva cocycle but tracks the sign that distinguishes a transversal hyperplane from a concurrency point:

1. **Forward direction.** With m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j, the twisted cocycle m(i,j)·m(j,k) = -m(i,k) and the 2-face product = -1 are direct field computations; the single extra minus per edge is what flips +1 into -1.
2. **Telescoping.** Writing m(i,j) = (-1)·(a_i/a_j) and applying ∏_{t<L} f(t)/f(t+1) = f(0)/f(L) along a closed walk gives signed product (-1)^L · 1, so odd cycles (triangles) give -1 and even cycles return to +1.
3. **Cube relation forces normalization.** From the 2-face conditions alone, m(i,i)³ = -1 over ℝ forces m(i,i) = -1 (factor (x+1)(x²-x+1), second factor positive), then signed reciprocity m(i,k)·m(k,i) = 1, then the twisted cocycle by cancelling the nonzero factor m(k,i).
4. **Reconstruction.** Setting a_i = 1/m(b,i), the twisted cocycle m(b,i)·m(i,j) = -m(b,j) is exactly m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j.
5. **Duality.** m(i,j) = -r(j,i) for the parent edge ratio r, and the Menelaus 2-face product is the negation of the Ceva 2-face product — the sign is the entire difference between the two classical theorems.
keyInsights: Menelaus is Ceva with a sign: the signed edge ratio is m(i,j) = -r(j,i), and the 2-face product is -1 (collinear/transversal) instead of +1 (concurrent). The two classical theorems are one identity up to sign.
Concurrency is an honest 1-cocycle; a transversal is a TWISTED cocycle m(i,j)·m(j,k) = -m(i,k). The twist is exactly the extra orientation reversal a hyperplane forces on each edge it crosses.
In dimension n the single planar Menelaus equation is replaced by the Menelaus product = -1 on EVERY triangular 2-face; those 2-face conditions generate the whole twisted cocycle.

Realizability is reconstruction: a nonzero signed assignment comes from a transversal hyperplane iff it is a twisted coboundary m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j, with vertex values recovered explicitly as a_i = 1/m(b,i).
The cube relation m(i,i)³ = -1 (only real root -1) is the lone nonlinear step; it is what makes the 2-face conditions sufficient, the signed analogue of the parent's r(i,i)³ = 1.
The signed closed-walk product (-1)^L explains why even cycles of a simplex (e.g. the tetrahedron's 4-vertex loop) return to +1 while odd cycles (triangles) give the Menelaus -1.
prerequisites: Euclidean / projective geometry (transversals, signed ratios, collinearity)
Menelaus's and Ceva's theorems for triangles
Elementary group cohomology intuition (1-cocycles, coboundaries, and twisting on a graph)

conclusion: Menelaus's theorem is Ceva's with a sign. A hyperplane crossing an n-simplex assigns signed edge ratios m(i,j) = -a_i/a_j that satisfy a TWISTED cocycle m(i,j)·m(j,k) = -m(i,k) and multiply to -1 around every triangular 2-face — the exact negation of the parent's Ceva +1 for concurrent cevians. A transversal hyperplane realizing a nonzero signed assignment exists precisely when the Menelaus product equals -1 on every 2-face, and the hyperplane is reconstructed explicitly as a_i = 1/m(b,i). The closed-walk product (-1)^L unifies the triangle's -1 with the even cycles' +1. This completes the Ceva/Menelaus dual at the algebraic level of the parent's higher-dimensional Ceva entry, fully machine-checked with 0 axioms and 0 sorries.
